summary: Describes the messages and procedures of the NACK-Oriented Reliable Multicast (NORM) protocol. It provides end-to-end reliable transport of data objects or streams over IP multicast, with receivers asking for repairs by sending negative acknowledgments. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: NORM sends a file or a live stream to a group of receivers over IP multicast and makes sure everyone ends up with the whole thing. The trick is that receivers normally say nothing. Only when a receiver notices a gap does it ask for that piece to be sent again, and it waits a random time first so that a hundred receivers missing the same piece do not all ask at once.

questions: how does nack-oriented reliable multicast work
how does norm reliable multicast use nacks
how does norm congestion control work
subtitle: Reliable bulk data delivery to a multicast group, where receivers only speak up when something is missing.

tldr.problem: Sending a file to a multicast group needs every receiver to get it intact, but asking the sender to resend lost packets to everyone does not scale to large audiences.
tldr.mechanism: NORM uses forward error correction so most losses are repaired without asking, and receivers that are still missing data send a negative acknowledgement. Before sending it, a receiver waits a random time, so that many receivers missing the same data do not all ask at once.
tldr.outcome: The sender repairs most losses with parity data it already has, the receivers that did lose data get it back, and the group shares bandwidth fairly with TCP. The document replaced RFC 3940 in 2009.

today: RFC 5740 is a Proposed Standard on the IETF Standards Track. It replaced RFC 3940 in 2009 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The changes from the experimental version included an IANA registry for header extensions, removal of the restriction on receiver feedback rate, a description of a secure mode using IPsec, and the definition of the EXT_AUTH header extension.

sections.title: What NORM Does
sections.content:
NORM provides reliable transport of data from one or more senders to a group of receivers over an IP multicast network. The primary design goals are efficient, scalable and robust bulk data transfer, such as computer files or persistent data, across possibly heterogeneous IP networks and topologies. It supports distributed multicast session participation with minimal coordination among senders and receivers, and lets senders and receivers join and leave sessions at will with little overhead for control information and timing synchronisation.

Reliability comes from a selective negative acknowledgement mechanism, with forward error correction providing most of the repair. NORM is self-adapting to changing network conditions with little or no pre-configuration, and tolerates inaccurate timing estimates and lossy conditions, including mobile and wireless networks. It can also converge and maintain efficient operation under heavy packet loss and large queuing or transmission delays.

NORM must be able to operate end to end with no help from intermediate systems beyond basic IP multicast group management, routing and forwarding. It can use reciprocal multicast communication under the Any-Source Multicast model, and must also work in asymmetric topologies such as Source-Specific Multicast, where only a unicast return path is available from the receivers to the sender. It is compatible with IPv4 and IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The design goal is a protocol that a huge audience can use without the sender drowning in complaints. It works with plain multicast routing, it copes with lossy mobile links, and it needs no help from the network in between.

sections.title: Sessions, Nodes and Objects
sections.content:
A NORM session is made up of participants acting as senders and/or receivers. Senders transmit data content as NORM objects to the session address, and receivers try to receive that content reliably using negative acknowledgements to request repair. Each participant has a preselected unique 32-bit identifier, the NormNodeId; two values are reserved, zero for an invalid identifier and all ones for a wildcard.

Three kinds of content can be transported. NORM_OBJECT_DATA is static data held in the sender's memory, NORM_OBJECT_FILE is data in the sender's file system, and NORM_OBJECT_STREAM is an ongoing transmission of undefined length, analogous to the reliable stream service of TCP. The difference between the first two is only a hint to receivers about whether to allocate memory or file storage. NORM also allows a small amount of out-of-band data, sent as NORM_INFO messages, to be attached to the content so receivers can quickly see what is being transmitted.

All objects are logically segmented into FEC coding blocks and symbols for transmission, and a FEC encoding symbol corresponds directly to the payload of a NORM_DATA message. With systematic FEC codes the first symbols of a block are the original data and the rest are parity, which is generally sent in response to repair requests but may also be sent proactively. Objects are temporarily identified by the sender's NormNodeId, an instance identifier and a transport identifier, and the transport identifiers are assigned in increasing order and reused in long-lived sessions.

Because the protocol does not identify content globally, an application that needs that must manage it itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A session has senders, receivers and a shared address. The content being sent is called an object, and there are three kinds: a block of memory, a file, or an endless stream. The sender cuts objects into blocks and encodes them so that missing pieces can be rebuilt.

sections.title: The Common Message Header
sections.content:
Every NORM message begins with the same 64-bit header. The version field is 4 bits and is 1 for this specification; implementations should ignore messages with a different version. The type field is 4 bits and says which kind of message it is: NORM_INFO, NORM_DATA, NORM_CMD, NORM_NACK, NORM_ACK or NORM_REPORT. The hdr_len field is 8 bits and gives the number of 32-bit words in the header, which is how the presence of header extensions is signalled. The sequence field is 16 bits, and the source_id field is 32 bits and identifies the node that sent the message within the session.

The sequence field does two separate jobs. Senders must set it on sender messages so that receivers can estimate packet loss for congestion control, using a monotonically increasing number space; it is explicitly not used in the reliability procedures, where the object and FEC payload identifiers detect missing content. Receivers should set it to protect against replay attacks on their feedback messages, keeping a separate increasing number space for each destination they send feedback to.

Header extensions follow the base header of the message type and come before any payload. There are two formats, both starting with an 8-bit header extension type: a variable-length form for type values from 0 to 127, which carries a length field in multiples of 32-bit words, and a fixed-length form of one 32-bit word for type values from 128 to 255.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message starts the same way: which version, which kind of message, how long the header is, a counter and the identity of the sender. Optional extras are added after it, in one of two shapes depending on their length.

sections.title: Sender Messages
sections.content:
NORM_DATA is the message type senders use most, carrying the segmented content of objects of any of the three types. It has three parts: a fixed header, a FEC payload identifier whose format depends on the FEC code in use, and a payload holding source or encoded application data. For stream objects the payload also carries fields for recovering stream content. The base header length is four 32-bit words plus the size of the FEC payload identifier, and header extensions add to it.

NORM_INFO carries the small out-of-band information that describes the content, and its size must fit into the payload of a single message.

NORM_CMD carries protocol control functions rather than data. The document registers seven sub-types: FLUSH, which tells receivers to send any repair requests they have, EOT, which marks the end of the transmission of an object, SQUELCH, which tells receivers to stop asking for data the sender no longer has, CC, which carries congestion control information, REPAIR_ADV, which advertises the sender's accumulated repair state, ACK_REQ, which requests positive acknowledgements, and APPLICATION, which is left for applications to use.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of message come from the sender: the data itself, a small note describing what the data is, and control messages such as a request for repair or a congestion control update.

sections.title: How a Receiver Asks for Repair
sections.content:
When a receiver notices missing data it starts a NACKing procedure, and it may only start at FEC coding block boundaries, object boundaries, on receipt of a FLUSH command, or when transmissions from a previously active sender stop arriving. The recommended inactivity timeout is the robustness factor times twice the sender's advertised group round-trip time, with a minimum of one second, and receivers should rescale it as the advertised round-trip time changes.

The procedure begins with a random backoff timeout, chosen with the RandomBackoff algorithm of the Multicast NACK Building Block, using the sender's advertised round-trip time and group size. The backoff factor must be greater than one for effective feedback suppression, with 4 recommended for Any-Source Multicast and 6 for Source-Specific Multicast. If the backoff time comes out longer than (K_sender minus 1) times the round-trip time, the receiver suppresses its request entirely and enters a holdoff period, which avoids a NACK implosion when the sender or the network has failed.

Otherwise the receiver waits out the backoff, collecting repair state from NACK and REPAIR_ADV messages it hears from other receivers, and then sends its own NACK only if the sender has moved on past the receiver's earliest repair need and the accumulated state does not already cover it. The holdoff period afterwards lasts (K_sender plus 2) times the round-trip time.

The NACK message names the repair positions from the receiver's lowest ordinal need up to the block before the most recent position it heard. For a partially received block, the receiver first asks for the parity portion, starting from the lowest ordinal parity symbol and requesting as many symbols as its erasure count for that block. Later repair cycles ask only for the symbols it has not yet received. If the erasure count exceeds the parity available, it asks for all the parity plus the highest missing data segments, so that the whole receiver group ends up asking for the same set of symbols and the sender can send one efficient repair transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver that has lost something waits a random time before complaining, so that other receivers with the same gap complain at different moments and the sender only has to send the repair once. When it does complain, it names the exact pieces it needs.

sections.title: How the Sender Repairs
sections.content:
The sender's goal is to make forward progress on new data, but it sometimes has to rewind its logical transmission point to satisfy receivers that have asked for repair. When a NACK arrives while the sender is transmitting new data, it begins accumulating repair state, and this does not interrupt the ongoing transmission. The aggregation period lasts (K_sender plus 1) times the sender's estimate of the group's greatest round-trip time. When the period ends the sender folds the accumulated state into its pending transmission state and starts sending repairs, then resumes new data. It then holds off for one round-trip time before starting a new aggregation cycle, so that late NACKs are folded in rather than triggering a second repair wave.

The sender should use FEC parity for repair whenever it can. It can work out the maximum erasure-filling need for each coding block from the NACKs it received, and if it has enough unsent parity symbols for that block, it sends those instead of the specific packets the receivers asked for. Only when its supply of fresh parity is exhausted does it fall back to sending exactly what was requested. Repair transmissions are flagged as repairs, and explicit repairs carry a further flag so that receivers can apply their policies about new arrivals.

Two control messages complete the picture. If a NACK asks for data the sender no longer supports, the sender sends a SQUELCH message, at a rate of no more than once per two round-trip times, so that receivers stop asking for data that is gone. When receivers send their NACKs by unicast rather than to the group, the sender uses REPAIR_ADV messages, multicast to the group, to advertise its aggregated repair state, so receivers can suppress their own requests in the same way they would if they could hear each other.
sections.plainLanguage: When the sender gets repair requests it gathers them for a moment, then sends what is needed. It prefers to send parity data it has already computed, because one parity packet can fix a gap for everyone at once, instead of the exact packets each receiver asked for.

sections.title: Congestion Control
sections.content:
NORM specifies a baseline congestion control scheme, NORM-CC, adapted from the equation-based TCP-Friendly Multicast Congestion Control approach. It is required for operation within the general Internet unless the implementation is adapted to use another IETF-sanctioned reliable multicast congestion control mechanism. The transmissions of NORM senders are controlled in a rate-based manner rather than with a window as TCP does, although the NORM message set could also support a window-based scheme.

Successful control depends on collecting sender-to-receiver loss estimates and round-trip times to identify the bottleneck paths in the topology. The receiver whose measurements give the lowest calculated sending rate is the current limiting receiver, and in a tie, where candidates are within 10% of the same rate, the receiver with the largest round-trip time should be chosen. The sender's rate is then computed from the standard TCP-friendly formula, using the size of the transmitted packets, the round-trip time of the current limiting receiver and its loss event fraction. In NORM the nominal packet size can be an exponentially weighted moving average of transmitted packet sizes, to account for varying message sizes.

The sender periodically transmits NORM_CMD(CC) messages alongside its data. They stimulate explicit feedback from the receivers, communicate the current congestion control status including the identity of the current limiting receiver, and ask for immediate feedback from that receiver so the sender can track the worst path closely. They can also ask for feedback from potential limiting receivers, receivers identified as likely to become the limiting one.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender measures the path to each receiver and works out which one is worst. It then slows down to the rate that worst path allows, using the same idea as TCP: back off when packets are being lost. One special message carries those measurements and asks the worst receiver to report back quickly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The same security considerations that apply to the Multicast NACK, TFMCC and FEC building blocks also apply to NORM. Beyond the vulnerabilities any IP protocol has, malicious hosts might engage in excessive NACKing to prevent the sender from making forward progress, and the receiver join and service policies can be applied when that is detected. Cryptographic peer authentication, integrity checks and confidentiality can give better protection, but even with them, the NACK-based feedback can be exploited by replay attacks that force the sender to transmit repair information unnecessarily. Network-layer IP security or the EXT_AUTH header extension can address this, and such mechanisms should be deployed when available.

Implementations are required to be compatible with IPsec usage. The ESP protocol or the Authentication Header extension can secure the IP packets carrying NORM messages, providing peer authentication, integrity protection and encryption. The EXT_AUTH header extension, with type 1, is reserved for security mechanisms as an alternative to IPsec; its format and processing are out of scope and communicated out of band, and it can also provide encryption of NORM message payloads. It can also be used where network address translation is in the way of the IPsec Authentication Header. If EXT_AUTH is present, the checks that can be done immediately on receipt must be done before the packet is accepted and before any congestion control action is taken, but security must not delay congestion control behaviour.

Consideration must also be given to replay attacks that transplant authenticated packets from one session to another, so unique keys should be assigned per session or unique instance identifiers used. The sequence field can be used to detect replay attacks when the sender keeps state on receivers that are actively asking for repair. Because NORM leverages FEC repair for scalability but that alone does not guarantee integrity, application-level integrity checking of received data is highly recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who can send packets can pretend to be a receiver in distress and make the sender waste bandwidth. The document asks for authenticated and encrypted messages where possible, and for the application to check the data it receives even when the transport looks secure.

fields.name: version
fields.desc: Protocol version number. The value for this specification is 1.

fields.name: type
fields.desc: The message type: NORM_INFO, NORM_DATA, NORM_CMD, NORM_NACK, NORM_ACK or NORM_REPORT.

fields.name: hdr_len
fields.desc: Number of 32-bit words in the header. A larger value than the base means header extensions are present.

fields.name: sequence
fields.desc: Set by the originator. Senders use it for loss estimation; receivers use it against replay attacks.

fields.name: source_id
fields.desc: The 32-bit identifier of the node that sent the message within the session.

items.label: NORM_INFO
items.desc: Out-of-band information about the content being sent.

items.label: NORM_DATA
items.desc: Segmented data content, source or FEC-encoded.

items.label: NORM_CMD(FLUSH)
items.desc: Tell receivers to send the repair requests they have.

items.label: NORM_CMD(EOT)
items.desc: Marks the end of transmission of an object.

items.label: NORM_CMD(SQUELCH)
items.desc: Stop asking for data the sender no longer has.

items.label: NORM_CMD(REPAIR_ADV)
items.desc: Advertises the sender's accumulated repair state.

items.title: Inactivity timeout
items.text: NORM_ROBUST_FACTOR times 2 times the sender's advertised round-trip time, with a minimum of 1 second.

items.title: Backoff
items.text: RandomBackoff with K_sender times the round-trip time as the maximum, and the advertised group size. K_sender is 4 for Any-Source Multicast and 6 for Source-Specific Multicast.
